Cumulative RMST bands for survival curves

Source: R/rmst_calculations.R
cumulative_rmst_bands.Rd

Calculates cumulative Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) and confidence bands for survival curves using resampling. Optionally plots the cumulative RMST curve, pointwise confidence intervals, and simultaneous confidence bands.

Usage

cumulative_rmst_bands(
  df,
  fit,
  tte.name,
  event.name,
  treat.name,
  weight.name = NULL,
  draws_sb = 1000,
  xlab = "months",
  ylim_pad = 0.5,
  rmst_max_legend = "left",
  rmst_max_cex = 0.7,
  plot = TRUE,
  mean_rule = c("trapezoid", "rectangle"),
  weight_variance = c("known", "estimated"),
  weight_model = NULL
)

Arguments

df

Data frame containing survival data.

fit

Survival fit object (output from KM_diff).

tte.name

Name of time-to-event variable in df.

event.name

Name of event indicator variable in df.

treat.name

Name of treatment group variable in df.

weight.name

Optional name of weights variable in df.

draws_sb

Number of resampling draws for simultaneous bands (default: 1000).

xlab

Label for x-axis (default: "months").

ylim_pad

Padding for y-axis limits (default: 0.5).

rmst_max_legend

Position for RMST legend (default: "left").

rmst_max_cex

Text size for RMST legend (default: 0.7).

plot

Logical; if TRUE, plot the results. Default is TRUE.

mean_rule

Character; how the survival difference is integrated over the time grid of fit (fit$at_points). "trapezoid" (default) averages the difference at consecutive grid points: \(R(t_j) = \sum_{k \le j} \{d(t_{k-1}) + d(t_k)\}/2 \, (t_k - t_{k-1})\). "rectangle" is the left-rectangle sum \(R(t_j) = \sum_{k \le j} d(t_{k-1}) (t_k - t_{k-1})\), the exact area under the step function. In both, \(R = 0\) at the first grid point. "rectangle" equals the difference of survfit()'s restricted means (summary(fit, rmean = tau)) when the time grid holds every event time, which it does for the default KM_diff() grid; it does not when the fit was made with modify_tau = TRUE. The rule applies to the estimate and to both sets of resampled curves; nothing else changes.

weight_variance

How the weights are treated in standard errors, intervals, bands and tests. "known" (default): as fixed, known numbers. "estimated": as estimated by the logistic propensity model given in weight_model, whose estimation is carried into the inference. Estimates never change. See the section "Estimated weights".

weight_model

With weight_variance = "estimated", the object returned by ps_weights for the rows of df, in the same order; its weights must be the column weight.name. Ignored with "known".

Value

A list with elements:

at_points

Time points used for RMST calculation

rmst_time

Cumulative RMST estimates

sig2_rmst_time

Variance of RMST estimates

rmst_time_lower

Pointwise lower confidence interval

rmst_time_upper

Pointwise upper confidence interval

rmst_maxtau_ci

RMST and CI at maximum time

rmst_text

Text summary for legend

c_alpha_band

Critical value for simultaneous band

rmst_time_sb_lower

Simultaneous band lower bound

rmst_time_sb_upper

Simultaneous band upper bound

mean_rule

The integration rule used

weight_variance

"known" or "estimated": how the weights were treated

Details

The pointwise variance of the cumulative RMST difference and the simultaneous band come from the resampled survival-difference curves of fit (fit$dhat_star) and of a second KM_diff call with seedstart = 99999. With weights that are not all equal, those resampled curves are built from the per-subject contributions of the robust variance (see resampling_survival), so the RMST variance and bands are the robust ones; with no weights or all weights equal they are unchanged. By default the weights are treated as fixed and known. For weights estimated by a logistic propensity model, weight_variance = "estimated" (with the same option in the KM_diff() call that made fit; a fit made with the other option is an error) carries their estimation into both sets of resampled curves, and so into the variance, the intervals and the band (section "Estimated weights"). With extreme weights (low effective sample size) the intervals can be too narrow under either option.

Estimated weights

Propensity-score weights are estimated from the data. weight_variance says how standard errors, intervals, bands and tests treat them.

"known" (default)

The weights are fixed, known numbers: the formulas of the two sections above. weight_model is ignored.

"estimated"

The weights were estimated by a logistic regression for the treatment, given as weight_model (the object returned by ps_weights), and that estimation is carried into the inference.

Estimates never change: survival curves, their difference, RMST, the log-rank score, hazard ratios, counts and risk tables are identical under the two options. Only standard errors, intervals, bands and tests differ.

Notation. There are \(n\) subjects, the rows analysed. Subject \(i\) has arm \(A_i\), row \(x_i\) of the model matrix of the propensity model (\(p\) columns), fitted probability \(e_i\) and weight \(w_i\) (written \(a_i\) in the score formulas above). The influence of subject \(i\) on the fitted coefficients and the derivative of its weight in the coefficients are $$IF_i = \Big\{\sum_j x_j x_j' e_j (1 - e_j)\Big\}^{-1} x_i (A_i - e_i), \qquad dw_i = -\frac{1 - e_i}{e_i} x_i \ (A_i = 1), \quad dw_i = \frac{e_i}{1 - e_i} x_i \ (A_i = 0)$$ (for stabilised weights \(w_i\) and \(dw_i\) are multiplied by the arm proportion).

Kaplan-Meier estimate of a group \(g\) (an arm; an arm within a stratum; all subjects). With \(\psi_i(t)\) the influence value of the section "Variance of the Kaplan-Meier estimate", computed from the group's own weighted counts, $$D_g(t) = \sum_{k \in g} \psi_k(t)\, dw_k, \qquad \Phi_i(t) = 1(i \in g)\, w_i \psi_i(t) + IF_i' D_g(t) \quad (i = 1, \ldots, n),$$ $$\widehat{Var}[\hat S_g(t)] = \hat S_g(t)^2 \sum_{i=1}^n \Phi_i(t)^2.$$ Every subject contributes, also those outside the group, through the model. The variance of the difference of the two arms is $$\widehat{Var}[\hat S_1(t) - \hat S_0(t)] = \sum_{i=1}^n \{\hat S_1(t) \Phi^1_i(t) - \hat S_0(t) \Phi^0_i(t)\}^2,$$ which is not the sum of the two arm variances: the arms share the model's coefficients. A resampled curve of arm \(a\) is \(-\hat S_a(t) \sum_{i=1}^n G_i \Phi^a_i(t)\) with the standard-normal multipliers \(G_i\) that KM_diff generates in any case; the resampled difference curves, the simultaneous band and the RMST variance and band of cumulative_rmst_bands follow from them unchanged.

Score of the log-rank test and of the weighted Cox estimate. With \(\psi_i(\beta)\) the contribution of the section "Variance of the log-rank and Cox score with subject weights", computed within each stratum, $$B(\beta) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\psi_j(\beta)}{a_j}\, dw_j, \qquad \psi^{ew}_i(\beta) = \psi_i(\beta) + IF_i' B(\beta), \qquad \widehat{Var}\{U(\beta)\} = \sum_{i=1}^n \psi^{ew}_i(\beta)^2.$$ The log-rank z-score, the variance of the log hazard ratio estimate (the sum at \(\hat\beta\) over the squared information) and a resampled score (\(-\sum_i G_i \psi^{ew}_i(\beta)\)) are formed as before with \(\psi^{ew}\) in place of \(\psi\). In a stratified analysis the variance is this single sum over all subjects, not a sum of per-stratum variances. The cumulative variance of wlr_cumulative is \(\sum_i \{c_i(t) + IF_i' B(t)\}^2\) with \(c_i(t)\) the contribution of subject \(i\) to the score up to \(t\) and \(B(t) = \sum_j \{c_j(t) / a_j\} dw_j\); in wlr_dhat_estimates the contribution to the survival difference is \(d_i + IF_i' (\hat S_0 D_0 - \hat S_1 D_1)\) at the grid point read for tzero, and the covariance uses both adjusted contributions. The outputs of df_counting() that come from the survival package (logrank_results, cox_results$score, $se, $hr_ci, $pval) carry the same adjustment, applied to coxph()'s weighted score and dfbeta residuals \(r\): \(r_i + IF_i' \sum_j (r_j / w_j) dw_j\).

How to use it. Fit the propensity model on exactly the rows to be analysed with ps_weights, put its weights in a column of df, and pass weight_variance = "estimated" and weight_model to df_counting(), KM_diff, cumulative_rmst_bands or plotKM.band_subgroups. cox_rhogamma, wlr_cumulative and wlr_dhat_estimates take the option from the df_counting() result they are given (its elements weight_variance and ew_parts). The rows of df, the treatment column and the weight column must be those of weight_model; anything else is an error.

Scope and limits of this version.

  • A logistic glm for a binary treatment, fitted on exactly the rows analysed. For weights from any other model use "known".

  • A subgroup analysis that reuses weights from a model fitted on the full sample must use "known": the model's rows are then not the rows analysed. (The subgroup curves of plotKM.band_subgroups() are point estimates and are not affected.)

  • draws > 0 (the resampling-based pointwise variance) is not available with "estimated"; draws.band and the resampling of cox_rhogamma() are.

  • The time weights of the scheme (Fleming-Harrington and the others) depend on the weighted pooled curve; that dependence on the estimated weights is ignored.

  • With stabilised weights the arm proportion is treated as a fixed number. The Kaplan-Meier quantities do not depend on that: they are unchanged when an arm's weights are multiplied by a constant.

  • With "estimated" the influence-based formulas always run; whether the weights are all equal is not tested.

  • Carrying the estimation through does not repair extreme weights: when the effective sample size (df_counting()$ess) is a small fraction of an arm, standard errors, intervals and tests can be too optimistic under either option.

The device of carrying the estimation of a nuisance quantity into the inference by perturbing its estimate is that of Leon, Cai and Wei (2009); it is used here in linearised form.
